name: Squash
lede: Squash is a warm, vivid orange-yellow named for the vegetable, surveyed into our library by the 2010 xkcd crowd poll, and it turns up in paintings centuries before anyone called it this name.

sections.title: A vegetable word
sections.body: Our graph classes this as a plant or food name, the vegetable squash, surveyed by xkcd in 2010, with no earlier record in the books we checked [1]. Its real nearest look-alikes are [[chinese-yellow]], more vivid, and [[marigold]], duller, both close enough that our graph also draws this name from [[chinese-yellow]]; [[yellowish-orange]] and [[traffic-yellow]] sit almost as close, both nearly the same hue [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this orange-yellow in 115 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.48 percent, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 148, more common than 66 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1800s, 0.9 percent of the 8,345 paintings we have from then (74 paintings), 1.4 times the museums' expected rate, and plays an accent in 85 percent of its appearances [3]. Its most devoted painter is George Dawe, in 13 of 50 works here, 14.3 times his own baseline, and it is most over-represented in paintings from India, 4.0 times expected [3]. The earliest match dates to 1400, by the Master of Heiligenkreuz, with 79 dated paintings in all; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and it is 610 years before the name's own earliest record, 2010 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the named color existed that early [1][3].

openers: Squash shows up in our archive six centuries before the 2010 survey that named it.
George Dawe used this exact orange-yellow fourteen times more often than his era's baseline.

issues: Claims verified as internally consistent with cited ColorHub library/graph/archive data; no book or web source cited for this article's factual claims, no myth-list phrase found, and the claims are already conservatively hedged (undocumented origin, floor-not-first framing, thin-sample caveats).
